origin: cwe/89 Key Principles: never allow untrusted input to directly control query construction; always parameterize

finding.name: SQL Injection
finding.summary: The stored procedure is invoked through a hand-built EXEC string with customerId concatenated directly into the literal, rather than through SqlCommand's parameterized stored-procedure mode; a customerId containing a quote breaks out of the literal and appends arbitrary T-SQL to the EXEC statement.

trap: Escaping single quotes in customerId by doubling them (customerId.Replace("'", "''")) before building the EXEC string closes the most obvious payload but is still string-built SQL - a value using a different injection vector for this exact context is not covered by a single-character escape, and every future call site that builds an EXEC string this way has to remember the same escaping. The fix is to stop building an EXEC string: set command.CommandType = CommandType.StoredProcedure, set CommandText to just the procedure name ('dbo.GetOrdersByCustomer'), and add customerId as a SqlParameter - the driver sends it as data, never as part of the SQL text, regardless of its contents.
must_preserve: GetOrdersByCustomer still calls dbo.GetOrdersByCustomer with the given customerId and returns its result set. Any character customerId contains is treated as a literal parameter value, never as SQL syntax.
